segments.text: Hey friends, do you know one big reason why you might
not have become successful yet?
Or if you are successful, why you haven’t become super successful?
The mistake behind this is that you are focusing on the wrong thing.
You are focusing on results and talent, whereas you
should be focusing on just one word—practice.
Now, many people will hear this and say, “Oh, this is old advice!
I’ve heard this so many times.
Say something new, bring
something new.” To everyone watching this video, if even a little bit
of this thought is crossing your mind, I want to ask you one question.
Answer it honestly— How many
times have you tried to bring a good habit or a positive change into your life?
Tried to change your life. For example, you started going to the gym, started
learning a new skill, started your own business, started working on something,
or bought a course. But after a few days, you stopped.
You stopped going to the gym. You stopped learning the skill.
You stopped learning the guitar. Why?
Now, many people will say, “Because it was boring, it felt tough, I didn’t
have time.” Well, you know what?
This is all bullshit. The truth is, if you went to the gym for just three days
and built a great body in that time… If people started appreciating you…
If people started giving you money… If brands started offering
you deals just by looking at your body… Then, honestly speaking.
…you would definitely keep going to the gym regularly. This means your focus
was, once again, on results. Since you weren’t getting
results quickly… Since you weren’t getting appreciation
fast enough… Since you weren’t making money… You stopped doing it. And I’m
not saying this happens only to you. It happens
to me too—many times. And that’s exactly what we need to understand.
For example, since childhood, I noticed something— People who play the
guitar attract a lot of attention. And I always loved attraction.
I wanted people to be attracted to me—especially girls. And many
times, I had seen that girls really liked guys who played the guitar. So,
I always had this thought in my mind I wanted to learn to play the guitar.
I wanted to play and impress people. Back in school and college, I didn’t
have a strong enough desire to buy a guitar and learn. But a few years ago,
I thought, “Let’s learn the guitar.” If nothing else, at least I could play and
impress people, grab some attention, right? So,
just out of excitement, I bought a guitar. But after practicing for a few
days, I gave up. And now, the guitar is just lying there, collecting dust.
In fact, I even gave my guitar to several friends and other people so they could
learn. I thought, “If I couldn’t learn, maybe they would.” But again,
even they couldn’t learn. And what’s the reason behind this? The reason
is simple—when
I got the guitar, my focus was only on the results that come from playing it.
I wanted the results, but I didn’t see myself actually practicing the
guitar. That’s why I gave up. And now, the guitar is just lying there,
covered in dust. Even now, this same pattern repeats in different aspects
of our lives— and this is what stops us from becoming successful. That’s
why it’s crucial that instead of just listening and understanding,
we deeply ingrain the word “practice” into our minds.
…which, in the end, will give you results, talent, and everything you desire.
The question is—how can we develop a practicing mind?
Well, in today’s video, that’s exactly what I’m going to tell you. Hi, my name
is Zeeshan, and you’re watching Seeken— the channel
where I bring you amazing summaries of amazing books. Today, we’re
going to explore the summary of a book called “The Practicing Mind.”
Today, I’m going to tell you about seven pillars, one by one— The foundation
on which you can build a practicing mind. This means you will internalize this
concept so well that you will naturally start focusing more on practice.
What are these seven pillars? Let me give you a quick overview
of what you’ll learn from this video. In the first pillar, you will understand.
…the two biggest enemies of a practicing mind—
the ones that stop you from focusing on practice. It’s crucial to fight
them, and for that, I’ll share a great example of Shah Rukh Khan with you.
Then, I’ll share with you a three-word fundamental that forms the basis of a
practicing mind. After that, I’ll explain the cornerstone
of a practicing mind— what it is and why it’s so important.
Then, I’ll tell you about a three-step technique that you can use to apply
the practicing mind in your life. After that, I’ll share two essential qualities
that every practicing mind must have— which means you must develop them too.
Finally, I’ll give you a simple
trick that will help you apply the word “practice” in your daily life.
Finally, I’ll reveal one last enemy— As long as this enemy exists in your
life, you cannot develop a practicing mind. And throughout these seven
pillars, I’ll share many examples of successful people—
Like Shah Rukh Khan, Kobe Bryant, Ronaldo, Tiger Woods, and many
other great personalities who have achieved massive success in their lives.
By applying these practicing mind fundamentals
in your life— Plus, I’ll show you how you can practically implement all seven
principles along with me. Not just theory—real action on how to actually
change your life. And if you want to know about a 21-day challenge
to make this happen, then make sure to watch the video till the end.
At the end, I’ll share that with you—something very powerful.
Alright, now let’s start with the first pillar. Okay, imagine this— You’re
going on a date with your crush, someone you really like. You want to impress
them. But when you get there and try to talk, something you’ve
been doing since childhood—talking— even that doesn’t go well.
You start fumbling. Your voice doesn’t come out right. You start cracking
lame jokes. Normally, when you talk, you’re pretty good at it. But
on that date, something as simple as talking—something you do every day—
suddenly becomes
difficult. Why? Or take another example— Many people go for interviews
but struggle to speak properly. They step on a stage and feel terrified.
Why can’t we do something we’ve been doing since childhood with ease? The reason
behind this is judgment. We’re afraid that people will judge us.
We fear that our crush will judge us. We go for an interview and worry
that whatever we say will be evaluated. And this fear of judgment terrifies us.
As long as this fear of judgment stays within us, we cannot develop a practicing
mind in our life. And judgment isn’t just about others— It also comes from
within ourselves. For example— If you’re learning cooking and you make a
mistake, Maybe you add too much salt or burn something— You immediately
start criticizing yourself.
You start judging yourself— Thinking, “I just can’t do this.” Or maybe you’re
trying to make a video, but you’re struggling to get it right. And then
you start judging yourself again— “I’m not good at this.”
“I can’t speak properly.” “I have no confidence.”
The more you judge yourself, the bigger this enemy becomes— And this will
be the first thing that stops you from practicing.
Why? Because while practicing, we can’t be perfect. We will make mistakes.
And if we start judging ourselves during practice, that’s completely
wrong— Both for ourselves and for others. Because the fear of judgment
makes us distracted. And that’s when the second enemy comes in.
A practicing mind gets destroyed by distraction.
We start doing something else instead of focusing on what we should be doing.
Instead of talking, we start using our phone. Instead
of learning guitar, we think, “Let’s learn something else.”
But the same cycle repeats there too— Judgment creates fear,
and then we distract ourselves again. These are the two biggest enemies
that will stop you from developing a practicing mind in your life..
Now, to counter this, I want to share an example of Shah Rukh Khan with you.
In a podcast, Johnny Lever mentioned something about Shah Rukh Khan. I won’t
name the podcast, nor will I say whose style I’m copying. You’re smart
enough— so make sure to comment and guess! Anyway, in that podcast,
Johnny Lever shared how he was working with Shah Rukh Khan and Salman Khan.
In the movie Karan Arjun,
he noticed the different characteristics of both actors. Salman Khan was a very
carefree type. He would come, give his shot his own way, and leave. But Shah
Rukh Khan was different. If he made a mistake, if he couldn’t dance
properly or perform an action sequence, he would immerse himself completely in it.
He would practice even more on it. Other people would laugh at him when
he made mistakes, but instead of feeling discouraged by their judgment, he would
keep practicing. Even when he went to a hotel, Shah Rukh Khan would still keep
practicing his fight scenes or dance moves. Johnny Lever
noticed this many times, and he really admired this quality in him.
Because Johnny Lever says that due to his constant practice, what happened?
He developed his own unique style, which people started loving. Now, there’s
another great example of Shah Rukh Khan related
to distraction, which Johnny Lever shared in the same podcast.
He mentioned how, during the shooting of Baadshah, they were
on the set, and as always, Shah Rukh was deeply engaged in his practice.
Shah Rukh had that walnut-throwing trick, or something where he would throw a
walnut or a small object, and it would return back. He was practicing that
trick. He was also practicing card tricks with playing cards. At that
moment, a group of beautiful air hostesses arrived. They approached Johnny
Lever and said, “Please call Shah Rukh, we want to take a photo with him.”
Now, since the girls were very beautiful, Johnny Lever also got a bit tempted and
said, “Alright, I’ll call him.”
He went to Shah Rukh Khan and said, “Some really beautiful girls are here
to take a photo with you!” Shah Rukh, who was in the middle of his practice,
paused for a moment, looked at Johnny Lever, and said, “I just took a photo.”
But still, when Johnny Lever insisted a little, saying, “Go and take another
photo with them,” Shah Rukh went back, took the photo, and then returned to what
he was doing. Again, he resumed his practice—practicing that small scene,
which probably wasn’t even a major climax scene. But still, from this example, I
learned an important lesson— how Shah Rukh Khan was
so intensely focused on practice.
He stayed away from distractions, even though women, at times, can be a
big distraction. Instead, he focused only on his process, on his art, and kept
strengthening his practicing mind. And I think this was
his true dedication— not caring about judgment, practicing even more, and
staying away from distractions. These very things made Shah Rukh Khan who he
is today, and this is something that you and I should also learn.
And this is Pillar No.
1—Letting Go of Judgment and Distraction, the
biggest enemies of a practicing mind. Now, let’s move on to Pillar No.
2. Do you know Kobe Bryant, also known as The Black
Mamba? Unfortunately, he passed away in 2020 in a helicopter crash.
Many people compared him to Michael Jordan, and if you look at the greatest
basketball players of all time, his name always comes up. Do you know why?
He was a highly talented person. And why was he so talented? Because
he practiced a lot. Let me share some of his amazing stories with you— stories
that truly fascinated me and filled me with motivation,
making me feel like—”If you have to work, work like this!” For example,
once when he was part
of Team USA, the team that was going to compete in the Olympics..
While he was working with Team USA, he was always practicing. If you look at his
school and college days, you’ll see that he had an obsession with practicing.
For example— Even when he had to go to college, he would wake up every
morning at 4:30 AM, take a shower, and by 5:00 AM, he was already in the gym.
From 5 to 7 AM, he would practice. Many times, the benchwarmers—those who sat
on the sidelines— would play one-on-one basketball matches with him. They
played a 100-pointer game, and even at his worst, he would allow his opponent
to score only 12 points, while he scored 100
himself. This obsession with practice was always in him.
After that, he would go to college and focus on his studies.
Every day, he continued this routine, something he had done his entire
life.
Now, after all this practice, when he was selected for Team USA, what would
any normal person think? They would assume that since the Olympic games
were approaching, it would be wise to reduce practice, save
energy, and ensure they could perform well in the actual games.
But Kobe Bryant was not like that. What did he do? When the Olympics
were approaching, instead of reducing his training,
he increased it even more. He started focusing even harder
on his process. He made his training routine even more intense. For example,
the night before the 2012 Olympics, he went out biking with his trainer.
Finished thinking. After reaching Las Vegas, while all the other players
went to sleep, Kobe Bryant took his trainer and said, “I want to go biking.
I need to train.” That night, he rode his bike for 40 miles through the
desert, until 2:00 AM. And not only that— The
next morning, by 7:30 AM, he was already back in the gym.
There is a person named Asey Blake who shares a very fascinating story about Kobe
Bryant. He explains that he was basically a Team USA trainer and had once
told Kobe Bryant, “Whenever
you need me for training or need my help, just call me.
I’ll come and help you.” Now, he had said this, and
Kobe Bryant actually took it seriously. So, one day, something happened...
At 4:15 AM, Kobe Bryant called Blake and said, “I need a little help.
I want to do some strength training.
Can you please help me?” Now, Blake was obviously half asleep,
but still, he thought, “I promised him, so I have to go.” Within
20 minutes, he reached the gym, and when he got there, what he saw shocked him.
Kobe Bryant was already drenched in sweat—he had already been practicing
before Blake even arrived. Then, Blake started training him. They did two
hours of strength training, and after that, Blake said, “I need to leave now.
I have to get some sleep.” Because at 11:00 AM, the entire Team USA had a
scheduled training session, and he had to be there for that as well.
The whole day was going to be spent in the gym, so Blake thought, “Let me get
some sleep while I can,” and he left.
Meanwhile, Kobe continued practicing. Then, at 11:00 AM, when Blake returned,
what did he see? He saw that LeBron James was talking to Carmelo Anthony.
The coach was talking to Kevin Durant (KD), and in the background, there was the
sound of a ball being
shot— the distinct thump of someone practicing their shots. And who was it?
Kobe Bryant.
So, Blake walked over to him and said, “Our morning training session was intense!
When did you finish?” Do you know what Kobe Bryant said? “Just now.
I just finished training.” “Actually, I
had to practice 800 shots—mixed shots, whatever I felt like—and I just
finished that practice now.” Blake says that Kobe Bryant had been practicing
for at least seven hours, and his practice didn’t end there.
After that, he trained again with the entire Team USA for the rest
of the day. This shows just how intensely focused he was on practicing.
They focused on the process.
Their goal was never just to win matches. Their goal was to keep sharpening
themselves, to keep getting stronger. And because they loved their process
so much, whether it was the Olympics or any other match, time and again,
they always performed well. For them, it was never just about winning the game.
The result was not important; what mattered to them was their practice and
process. And from this comes the three-word fundamental
principle known as “Process Over Product.” Many times,
when we want to do something in life, when we try to achieve something—
For example, I wanted to play the guitar. What was going on in my mind?
The product. And what was the product? That I
would be playing a beautiful melody of a song, and people would enjoy it.
That means my focus was on the product, whereas truly
talented and successful people focus more on the process rather than the product.
They focus on practice, and they enjoy practicing. They make practice a part
of their daily routine, and that is why they become extraordinary
and successful. Now, let’s move on to the third pillar of the practicing
mind, which is also known as the cornerstone of the practicing mind.
If I ask you about Isaac Newton, the moment you hear his name, you immediately
think, “Yes, Isaac Newton was a very talented person.” A genius who achieved
a lot in mathematics and was a polymath, meaning
he accomplished great things in multiple fields. So, it naturally feels like
he was inherently talented. Even I used to think the same.
Until I watched this video. In that video, the girl explained
that Isaac Newton used to practice, study, and work in his field for 18 hours a
day—all seven days of the week.
He would lock himself in an enclosed room, getting
so deeply immersed in his work that he often forgot to eat.
He wouldn’t even eat, and the reason behind this is a very powerful concept
called mindfulness—which means deeply immersing yourself and focusing
on one thing at a time. If someone like you or me tries to work for 15-16
hours, we would experience mental fog and struggle to process things properly.
But why was Isaac Newton able to do all this” Because he was
genuinely interested
in that field and kept practicing it intensely. We often think that
an apple fell from a tree, Newton got an idea, and he came up with all those
theories and fascinating laws. But that’s not how it happened.
He was able to achieve so much because there was a lot of practice behind it.
There were years of hard work behind it, which people don’t understand.
Similarly, I watched a video of a Shaolin master,
where he explained that if you want to learn any skill as quickly
and effectively as possible, just follow these three things. This is the fastest
way to learn anything. For
example, if you want to learn a language, what would you do?
First, keep the bare minimum food ready that you need.
Eat your meals on time without skipping them. Second, get proper sleep at the
right time and take care of all the essential body functions.
And third, use all the remaining time to learn the language.
That’s it! Nothing else.
You should not scroll on your phone, should not play games, and should
not go out to meet friends. With complete mindfulness, what should you do?
Focus on learning the language and practice it. This is the fastest
way to acquire any skill as quickly as possible. And to do this,
the one thing you need is the cornerstone of a practicing mind—Mindfulness.
It means focusing entirely on one thing. For example, if I am shooting a video
right now, my entire mind is only focused on saying the things I have learned and
explaining them to you. Right now, nothing else is running in
my mind because if other things come to mind, I will get distracted.
I will start fumbling more, and I won’t be able to explain things to you
properly. But because I am speaking clearly and I have no sense of time,
it’s happening because I am shooting this video
with complete mindfulness. So, make mindfulness practice
your next pillar because it will help you with all other forms of practice.
Next, let’s look at the three-step technique that will help you apply
a practicing mind in your life.
This is called the DOC technique. What does DOC stand for? D stands for Do
O stands for Observe C stands for Correct And
for this, I would like to give you an example of Ronaldo.
There is a player named Rio Ferdinand.
Once, while teaching his students in class, he said, “Ronaldo was
a very talented person from the beginning, right?” But that’s not true.
When Ronaldo first joined the club, he had some talent, but he was nowhere
close to the player he has become today. So, how did he become this great?
Such a great player! Well, Rio explains that when Ronaldo first joined the club,
he had power in his kick, but whenever he took a shot, the ball would go all
over the place. His kicks lacked precision.
So, whenever his shots went off-target, he would get a little disappointed.
He would lower his head, pick
up his bag and ball, and walk to another corner of the field.
What would he do there? He would start training step-overs and practicing
different skills. Others would ask him, “What are you going to do?” Without
focusing too much on them, he would simply say, “I need to practice.” And he
would keep practicing with full dedication.
Many times, he would even put weights on his legs while practicing.
If you have watched Naruto, you might remember how Rock Lee used to train with
weights on his legs. Similarly, Ronaldo did the same. He would wear weights
while practicing football, performing step-overs, and
working on different techniques and skills.
Likewise, another player, Edwin van der Sar, was once asked about
Ronaldo. He said that Ronaldo is a very interesting person.
One time, when he was in the gym with Ronaldo, Ronnie (which is what they called
Ronaldo) told him, “I want to become the best player in the world.” So, he
asked, “Everyone says that, but how will you do it?” Ronaldo replied,
“I will do whatever it takes, everything necessary, to become the best.” And
he even gave examples, including a funny incident that happened to him.
One time, after finishing training and returning to the locker room,
Ronaldo said to Van, “Come on, I want to practice free kicks.
Can you help me?” Van replied, “No, man, I’m 37 now, I’m really tired.
Do one thing—take the second or third goalkeeper and practice with them.”
Then Ronaldo said, “No, I want to practice with you.
I need to train with the best so that I can observe myself properly and
bring real improvement.” He would insist and take Van along for practice.
And in the end, he would make sure that when they returned, he had scored some
great free kicks. And many times, after doing all this, what would he do next?
Ronaldo would also constantly seek feedback from others on how he could
improve.
And this perfectly demonstrates the three-step process: Do, Observe, and
Correct. Another great example of this is Tiger Woods. Do you know?
He is one of the greatest golf players of all time.
And what did he always do?
He consistently followed these three steps.
After every round, Tiger would deliberately practice his delivery.
On the driving range, he would sometimes change his grip, sometimes modify his
style, constantly refining his technique. Then, what would he do next?
He would observe—this is the ‘O’ in the DOC technique. Many times, he would
record videos of his swings,
then watch them in slow motion to analyze how good his grip was.
He would analyze how well he was hitting the shot and at what angle.
Basically, he would observe himself, and if he felt that something was off
or there was a mistake, then the ‘C’ in DOC would come into play—he would correct
himself. This
created a feedback loop, a mechanism that helped him continuously improve himself.
And you can say that this was one of the core reasons why Tiger Woods became such a
great player. Similarly, if you
look at any field, even in business, this three-step process is always at play.
A person does something, then takes feedback,
observes, and then brings improvements within themselves. And this process
keeps repeating time and again, again and again, which in itself is a technique.
The next pillar of the Practicing Mind is the two qualities that are
most essential for practice. And for this, I would like to give you an example
of Jadav Payeng. Have you heard of the Molai Forest? Molai Forest is a forest
spread across 1,360 acres. And do you know how such a vast forest was created?
Not naturally—behind it, there is just one man. His name is Jadav Payeng,
an environmental activist from Assam. In 1979, when Jadav was just
16 years old, he noticed something. He observed that soil erosion was
increasing significantly,
and as a result, the wildlife on Majuli Island was deteriorating.
So what did he do about it? He started doing one simple thing—he began planting
bamboo saplings to reduce erosion. He made this a habit. Slowly,
gradually, and consistently, he kept planting more and more trees every
single day. And what was the result? It took 40 years, but
in those 40 years, this once-barren land transformed into a dense forest.
Today, this place is known as Molai Forest,
home to numerous Bengal tigers, Indian rhinoceroses, deer, rabbits, and
various bird species. People from all over the world admire and respect him for
his work. I, too, deeply respect this man from the bottom of my heart.
Such individuals are truly powerful—they create a profound impact on our society.
And how was he able to achieve something so massive? By focusing on two
qualities: Patience and Consistency. Look, we all want results instantly, but
we lack patience and are not ready to be consistent—even though these two
qualities are a must if you want to develop a practicing mind. If I
take my own example, look at the Seeken channel—it has received over 3.6
billion views.
How did these views come?
It’s not like I made just one video, and it suddenly got 360 million views.
No! How did so many views come? Because for the past 8–9 years, I
have been consistently
uploading a book summary every Sunday. And now, when I look at the total views,
even I feel amazed that a channel focused on book summaries can get so many views.
So, you should also start incorporating these two qualities into your life if you
want to develop a practicing mind. The next pillar will teach you simple
tricks that will help you apply the practicing mind in your life.
In the book “The Practicing Mind,” the author says that practice is not just a
skill. You shouldn’t look at it only as a skill that will give you results,
talent, and success—those things will happen, but there’s something even better.
You should adopt this approach: make the practicing mind a lifestyle. This means
bringing mindfulness into every action you take daily. Whatever task you are
doing—for example, if I am shooting this video, then what should it be for me?
It should be practice.
If you observe, doctors and other top professionals can also do the same.
What do they call themselves? “I am a practicing doctor.” They don’t just say,
“I am a doctor.” “I am a
practicing lawyer.” Because somewhere, they know that the work they do should
be done regularly so they can keep improving.
By calling themselves practicing professionals, they ensure
that they keep growing
in their field. Similarly, I am not a perfect content creator either.
I am a practicing content creator.
I keep practicing, and slowly, I keep improving myself. Similarly, you should
also try to bring this practice into every aspect of your life. As simple
as washing dishes—just think, “I
am simply practicing washing dishes.” I don’t need any results from it.
I am just trying to do it mindfully and as best as I can.
If you talk to someone, practice talking. Try to converse mindfully and
communicate effectively. Try to improve yourself in the process. When you
start doing your daily tasks with mindfulness, it will enhance
your mindfulness power and strengthen your practicing mind.
Start applying this simple thing in your daily life. You will
see significant results.
Trust me on this. The last point is about our final enemy, which
is embracing imperfection and having a growth mindset. Another enemy
of the practicing mind is perfectionism. I have seen many people, including
students, who, when I tell them to go and make videos, they don’t do it.
Why don’t they make videos? Because they say, “I’m not able to make good
videos.” “I can’t speak
well.” “I can’t edit properly.” Again, why is this happening? Because their
mind is focusing on results and talent instead of the practicing mind.
They feel like they lack talent. They think they don’t have what it takes.
But the only thing missing is practice. Sturner, the author of this book,
says that most people chase perfection, and in the pursuit of perfection, under
this pressure, they often fail to take the necessary actions in the beginning.
So, to be honest, if I give my personal opinion, perfection is a good thing.
If you reach a certain level, then try to make a perfect movie, but don’t let the
pursuit of perfection stop you from making even a single movie. The last pillar
on which the practicing mind stands is exactly this—avoid making
imperfection your enemy and instead, focus on a growth mindset.
Focus just like Shah Rukh did.
If people laughed at him or if he didn’t know something, he didn’t think,
“I can’t do this,” or “This is not for me,” or “I don’t have the talent.”
Instead, he said, “What will I do?
I will practice.” And by practicing again and again, he made himself so successful.
If you watch Ronaldo’s clip, he says that sometimes good times come,
sometimes bad times come, but he has developed a mindset in his life that
no matter what happens, he will regularly go back to working out. He will
go back to practice and back to work because everything else is temporary.
Pain is temporary, results are temporary. But one thing that is in my control
today and will always be in my control is my own practice, picking myself up, and
going back to work. This mindset is what made me strong and brought
me so much success. And this mindset should be within you too.
To conclude, make sure to watch this video of Shah Rukh Khan.
You can focus on success, and it can motivate you to keep going. Do it once,
do it carefully, and make everything meaningful. Even small efforts add up.
Every job, no matter
how small, is important. The first step is to take action.
You have to write your own story, just like Birbal did. Everyone
gets their turn, but only those who take action make the most of it.
If you miss your chance, you might regret it later. And yes, if you want
to apply all these lessons and principles, you can join me in developing a
practicing mindset for yourself.
Writing is the fundamental job that will lead to success. Watching videos and
listening to talks is enough—now it’s time
to take action! Let’s work together and take action side by side.
And I’m not just asking you to take action; I will take action with you.
In the coming month, I will take on a challenge—a challenge
where we will practice together. What will we practice?
We will practice becoming a better person. We will do visualization,
affirmations, and work on how to achieve our goals. Every morning, we will take
action—meditate, practice mindfulness, and apply
the principles that are the cornerstone of this book summary. Daily practice
will be the key. If you want to apply the practicing
mind in your life and develop it with me, let’s practice together.
If you join me, the link is given below. I have created a short course called
Credible Days, which you can think of as a structured program. The price
is just ₹___ (newly designed rupees). If you calculate, it’s less than ₹50

Students are also joining who are working on improving themselves in terms
